prompt.brief: Design a scientific climate-data platform that ingests satellite imagery, runs geospatial analysis and climate models, and serves reproducible visualization dashboards over decades of observations.
successSignals: Separate immutable satellite scenes and derived raster products from catalog metadata, model runs, and dashboard caches.
Partition imagery by spatial tile, acquisition time, and collection so petabyte-scale processing can run in parallel.
Make geospatial jobs asynchronous, reproducible, and resumable while keeping small catalog and visualization queries fast.
Explain coordinate reference systems, missing scenes, quality masks, provenance, access control, and regional recovery.

functional: Ingest satellite scenes and station observations, validate metadata, and create searchable collections.
Run tiled raster transforms, temporal aggregations, and climate-model jobs with progress and reproducible outputs.
Display map layers, time series, provenance, quality flags, and exportable results for authorized users.
nonFunctional: Keep catalog and tile metadata reads below 300 ms p95; expose long-running model jobs asynchronously.
Process petabyte-scale archives without a single hot spatial tile or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed scene metadata or provenance; make tiled retries and duplicate ingestion safe.
Degrade safely when model workers or external imagery providers fail and preserve the last valid published layer.
scaleAssumptions: Petabyte-scale archive across decades of satellite scenes and derived products.
Partition by spatial tile, acquisition date, sensor, and collection; split popular tiles by time or resolution.
Keep raw scenes immutable, retain manifests and provenance, and cache only bounded metadata and rendered tiles.

architecture.title: Climate Data Analysis Platform data platform architecture
architecture.summary: Design a scientific climate-data platform that ingests satellite imagery, runs geospatial analysis and climate models, and serves reproducible visualization dashboards over decades of observations. The design preserves immutable source evidence and contracts, processes partitions with checkpointed batch or streaming jobs, and serves curated results with freshness and quality metadata.

deepDives.title: Schema evolution and data quality
points: Version climate data analysis platform contracts and make compatibility rules explicit for every producer and consumer.
Quarantine malformed partitions instead of poisoning the whole dataset.
Track row counts, null rates, duplicates, distribution changes, and policy violations by partition.

deepDives.title: Watermarks, late data, and exactly-once effects
points: Use source cursors and event-time watermarks for climate data analysis platform progress, not wall-clock assumptions.
Make checkpoints, output keys, and sink commits retry-safe under at-least-once delivery.
Document how late events revise windows, aggregates, or snapshots.

deepDives.title: Replay, lineage, and cost
points: Keep immutable climate data analysis platform raw evidence and code or schema versions so failed outputs can be reproduced.
Separate hot serving storage from cold retention and cap replay concurrency.
Measure freshness, backlog, compute cost, storage growth, and quality-gate failure rate.

tradeoffs.title: Streaming versus batch
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use streaming for freshness-critical climate data analysis platform paths and batch for backfills, compaction, and expensive recomputation.
tradeoffs.caution: Forcing every workload into streaming makes state, replay, and cost harder to operate.

tradeoffs.title: Raw retention versus curated-only storage
tradeoffs.recommendation: Retain enough immutable raw evidence for replay, audit, and correction, then tier or expire it according to policy.
tradeoffs.caution: Without raw evidence, a bad transformation can require an unreproducible emergency fix.

tradeoffs.title: Central warehouse versus domain-owned datasets
tradeoffs.recommendation: Centralize governance and discovery while letting domain owners own contracts and quality signals.
tradeoffs.caution: A single team owning every transformation becomes a delivery bottleneck and hides data ownership.

commonMistakes: Treating climate data analysis platform ingestion success as proof that downstream data is complete or correct.
Dropping late events or schema failures without a quarantine and replay path.
Using wall-clock processing time where event-time windows and watermarks are required.
Overwriting curated data in place without run, code, schema, or input lineage.
Ignoring backlog, freshness, quality, storage, and compute-cost signals until consumers report stale data.

followUps.question: How do you replay a failed climate data analysis platform partition?
followUps.answer: Retain source cursor and watermark, rerun a versioned transformation into an isolated output, validate quality, then atomically publish the replacement.

followUps.question: How do you handle schema changes?
followUps.answer: Register a new version, validate compatibility, dual-read or dual-write when needed, and expose the active contract to consumers.

followUps.question: What does exactly once mean here?
followUps.answer: It means the combination of durable checkpoints, deterministic output identities, and idempotent sinks prevents duplicate business effects; transport alone remains at least once.

rubric.description: The answer addresses the climate data analysis platform workflow, scale, latency, durability, authorization, and failure contract.
The answer identifies the authoritative climate data analysis platform state, versioning or deduplication boundary, and how derived views converge.
The answer partitions climate data analysis platform traffic, isolates hot keys, and moves fan-out, retries, or rebuilds behind bounded asynchronous work.
The answer names freshness, backlog, error, cost, and recovery signals tied to the climate data analysis platform user experience.
